content_units: Simple Will in England & Wales: 2026 Snapshot

For an unmarried person with no children, a will matters because an unmarried partner would not inherit automatically under intestacy rules, and specific gifts to charities plus the remainder to a niece are easiest to handle clearly in a written will.
Practical fit for your situation:
- You can usually make a   simple will   yourself if your wishes are straightforward.
- The biggest decision point in your case is   how the jointly owned flat is held  : this affects whether your share can pass under your will.
- Leaving fixed sums to   two charities   and the   residue   to your niece is a standard will structure.
Main Steps and Key Decision Points
Step   What to do   Main decision point   Can you do it yourself?   When a solicitor is worth it
1   List your estate   Confirm what you own: flat share, savings of   GBP 38,000  , personal items   Yes   If ownership is unclear or assets are mixed with someone else

2   Check the flat ownership   Find out whether you and your sibling own as   joint tenants   or   tenants in common     Partly   Yes, especially if you want your share to pass by will and title needs changing
3   Choose beneficiaries   Decide exact charity gifts and whether niece gets   everything left over   after debts/costs/gifts   Yes   If you want backup beneficiaries or detailed gift wording
4   Pick executors   Choose 1-2 reliable adults to deal with paperwork, banks, and distributions   Yes   If family dynamics are difficult or executor choice may be disputed
5   Add backups   Name substitute charities/niece replacement if a gift fails   Yes   Useful if charity mergers, closures, or family contingencies worry you
6   Draft the will   Include revocation clause, executor clause, charity legacies, residue clause, signatures   Yes   Strongly recommended if you want maximum certainty and clean legal wording
7   Sign and witness correctly   Sign with   2 witnesses present at the same time  ; witnesses should not benefit   Yes   If you want supervised execution to reduce risk of invalidity
8   Store and review   Keep original safe; tell executors where it is; review after property or family changes   Yes   If using a firm’s will storage or later making codicils/updates
What Your Will Would Usually Cover
A simple will for your facts would often be structured like this:
- Appoint your   executor(s)  .
- Revoke any earlier wills.
- Leave a fixed sum to   Charity 1  .
- Leave a fixed sum to   Charity 2  .
- Leave the   remainder of your estate   to your   niece  .
- Say who receives the residue if your niece dies before you.
- Include standard signing and witness wording.
Important drafting point:
- Charities should be identified carefully using their   full legal name  ,   registered charity number  , and address if possible.
- The gift to your niece should normally be the   residuary gift  , meaning what is left after debts, funeral costs, tax, and the charity gifts are paid.
The Flat: The Most Important Decision Point
Whether your share of the flat passes under your will depends on the ownership type:
-   Joint tenants
- On your death, your interest usually passes automatically to your sibling by survivorship.
- Your will normally   cannot leave your share of the flat to someone else   while it remains joint tenancy.
-   Tenants in common
- Your defined share forms part of your estate.
- Your will   can leave that share   under the will.
Why this matters for your plan:
- If you are content for the flat to pass automatically to your sibling, your will can still deal with your   savings and other assets  .
- If you want your share of the flat to benefit your niece or anyone else, a solicitor is often worth using to:
- confirm current ownership;
- consider   severing a joint tenancy   if appropriate;
- align the Land Registry position with your will.
What You Can Usually Do Yourself
If the flat position is already clear and you want a straightforward will, you can usually handle these parts yourself:
- Make a list of assets and estimated values.
- Choose your executor and a backup executor.
- Decide the   exact fixed amounts   for each charity.
- Gather the charities’ correct registered details.
- Decide who gets the residue: your niece.
- Add backup wording such as:
- if one charity no longer exists, gift to its successor or similar charitable purpose;
- if your niece dies before you, who gets the residue instead.
- Arrange proper signing with two independent witnesses.
- Store the original safely and tell your executor where it is.
Good practice for a DIY will:
- Use clear full names and addresses.
- Avoid ambiguous phrases like “my favourite charity”.
- Do not let a beneficiary or a beneficiary’s spouse/civil partner act as witness.
- Keep the original intact; do not staple notes to it after signing.
When Paying a Solicitor Is Sensible
A solicitor is particularly worth considering in any of these situations:
-   Unclear flat ownership
- You do not know whether it is joint tenants or tenants in common.
-   You want your share of the flat controlled by the will
- This is the biggest legal issue in your scenario.
-   You want tax-efficient charity drafting
- Charitable gifts are generally exempt from inheritance tax, and a solicitor can ensure wording is clean.
-   You want stronger protection against disputes
- Supervised drafting/execution can help if capacity or undue influence could ever be questioned.
-   You want contingency planning
- Substitute beneficiaries, disaster clauses, and charity-failure wording.
-   You have any non-standard wishes
- Conditions on gifts, trusts, occupation rights, or unequal treatment between relatives.
In practice, your case sounds   simple to moderate  :
-   Simple   if the will only covers savings/personal possessions and you are happy for the flat to pass automatically to your sibling.
-   Moderate   if the flat ownership needs checking or changing.
A Practical Drafting Outline for Your Situation
A clean structure could look like this:
Option 1: DIY-style simple will   Best if flat ownership is clear and wishes are straightforward   Lowest cost
GOV.UK wills
Option 2: Solicitor-reviewed simple will   Best balance of certainty and cost for charity gifts plus residue   Useful if you want the wording checked
Find solicitor
Option 3: Solicitor with property review   Best if the jointly owned flat may need legal change   Strongest option for avoiding mistakes
Property guidance
Suggested clause flow:
- Intro and revocation of prior wills
- Appointment of executor(s)
- Funeral wish clause if wanted
- Specific pecuniary gift to Charity A
- Specific pecuniary gift to Charity B
- Residue to niece
- Backup residue clause if niece dies before you
- Administrative powers
- Signature and witness attestation

Find a solicitor
